chapters.name: Chapter 1: Reading sources and how government works

lessons.title: Lesson 1: How the GED Social Studies test works
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: List the parts and tools of the GED Social Studies test and write a study plan with dates.
This lesson builds toward: Using the official GED website, you will list the parts, question types, time and tools of the GED Social Studies test and write a study plan with dates, with all three skill areas named and at least one study date each week until the test.
The GED has four tests: Math, Reasoning Through Language Arts, Science and Social Studies. You can take them one at a time. The GED Testing Service makes the test. Some states use another high school equivalency test, HiSET, so check which test your state uses.
On ged.com, the Social Studies test is listed as 70 minutes with no break. It covers three skill areas: reading for meaning in social studies, analyzing historical events and arguments, and using numbers and graphs in social studies. Questions are multiple choice, fill in the blank, drag and drop, select an area and drop-down.
You get an on-screen calculator and a calculator reference sheet, and ged.com says you may bring your own TI-30XS calculator to a test center. Ged.com says it is not a memorization test: you use the information given to draw conclusions.
Ged.com lists a passing score of 145 for each subject. Times and rules can change, so check ged.com before you book. Ged.com has free sample tests and an official practice test, GED Ready.
Step by step:
- Go to ged.com and read the Social Studies test page.
- Write down the time, the three skill areas and the tools you get.
- Take the free sample Social Studies test to see where you stand.
- Pick a target test week.
- Write at least one study date each week, with the skill you will practice.
Words to know:
- GED: a high school equivalency test; passing all four subjects earns a credential that many employers and colleges accept like a diploma.
- HiSET: another high school equivalency test that some states use.
- Civics: the study of government and the rights and duties of citizens.
- Economics: the study of how people make, buy, sell and use goods and money.
Official sources:
- GED Testing Service: test subjects (time, question types, calculator)
- GED Testing Service: Social Studies test
- GED Testing Service: scores
- GED Testing Service: free sample tests (English and Spanish)
- GED Ready, the official practice test
- HiSET, another high school equivalency test (official site)
Try it now: Open ged.com and take the free Social Studies sample test (or read the Social Studies page if you cannot take it now). Write your study plan: your target test week and one date each week with the skill you will practice: reading sources, government, history, or graphs. Keep it for the final task.
You can now name the parts and tools of the GED Social Studies test and follow a study plan with dates.

check.q: What does ged.com say about the Social Studies test?
options: It is not a memorization test
It is only about other countries
check.why: Ged.com says it is not a memorization test; you reason with the information given.

check.q: Which is one of the three skill areas on the test?
options: Using numbers and graphs in social studies
check.why: Ged.com lists reading for meaning, historical events and arguments, and numbers and graphs.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Sources, point of view, fact and opinion
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Identify the main idea, point of view, facts and opinions in a source.
This lesson builds toward: Given a primary or secondary source, you will identify the main idea, the author's point of view, and which statements are facts and which are opinions, pointing to the words that show each answer.
A primary source was made by someone who was there at the time: a letter, a speech, a law, a photo, a diary. A secondary source was made later by someone studying the event, like a textbook or a news analysis. Both are useful; primary sources show how people saw things then.
Point of view is how the author sees the topic, shaped by who they are and what they want. Ask: who wrote this, when, and why? A factory owner and a factory worker in 1900 might describe the same strike very differently.
A fact can be checked and proven true or false: "The 19th Amendment was ratified in 1920." An opinion is a belief or feeling: "It was the most important change in our history." Words like best, worst, should, important and I believe often signal an opinion.
Worked example. A 1910 newspaper ad: "Our new machines make 500 shirts a day. Every modern family should buy our shirts!" Fact: 500 shirts a day (it can be checked). Opinion: every family should buy them. Point of view: a business selling its product.
Step by step:
- Ask who made the source, when and why.
- Decide: primary (made at the time) or secondary (made later).
- Say the main idea in one sentence.
- Mark each statement fact (can be checked) or opinion (belief or judgment).
- Describe the author's point of view and what they want the reader to do or think.
Words to know:
- Primary source: something made at the time of an event by someone who was there.
- Secondary source: something made later by someone studying the event.
- Point of view: how an author sees a topic, shaped by who they are and what they want.
- Fact: a statement that can be checked and proven.
- Opinion: a belief, feeling or judgment.
Try it now: Practice: a 1935 letter from a farmer: "Dust storms buried our fields three times this spring. The government should help farmers like us before it is too late." 1) Primary or secondary? 2) One fact. 3) One opinion. 4) Point of view? Answers: 1) Primary: written at the time by someone there. 2) Dust storms buried the fields three times that spring. 3) The government should help farmers. 4) A struggling farmer asking for help.
You can now tell primary from secondary sources, describe point of view, and sort facts from opinions.

check.q: Which is a primary source about World War II?
options: A website summary written last year
A letter a soldier wrote home in 1944
check.why: It was made at the time by someone who was there.

options: That was the best law Congress ever passed.
check.why: "Best" is a judgment that cannot be proven.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: How the US government works
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Explain which branch of government acts in a scenario and how checks and balances apply.
This lesson builds toward: Given a short civics scenario, you will explain which branch of government acts and how checks and balances or a constitutional right apply, getting at least 4 of 5 right.
The US Constitution divides the federal government into three branches so that no person or group holds too much power. The legislative branch is Congress (the Senate and the House of Representatives); it makes laws. The executive branch is the president, the vice president and the cabinet; it carries out laws. The judicial branch is the Supreme Court and other federal courts; they interpret laws and decide if they conflict with the Constitution.
Checks and balances let each branch limit the others. The president can veto a bill passed by Congress. The Senate confirms or rejects the president's nominees, such as federal judges. The Supreme Court can overturn a law it finds unconstitutional. Congress can, in extreme cases, remove a president from office.
The Bill of Rights is the first ten amendments to the Constitution. It protects rights such as freedom of speech, religion, the press and assembly (First Amendment), and rights of people accused of crimes, such as a fair and speedy trial. Power is also shared between the federal government and the states; this is called federalism.
Worked example. "Congress passes a bill. The president vetoes it." Which check is this? The executive checking the legislative branch.
Step by step:
- Find who is acting: Congress, the president or a court.
- Name the branch: legislative, executive or judicial.
- Ask what power is being used: make, carry out or interpret laws.
- If one branch limits another, name the check.
- If a person's rights are involved, look for the right in the Bill of Rights.
Words to know:
- Constitution: the highest law of the United States; it sets up the government.
- Legislative branch: Congress; it makes laws.
- Executive branch: the president, vice president and cabinet; it carries out laws.
- Judicial branch: the courts; they interpret laws.
- Veto: when the president rejects a bill passed by Congress.
- Amendment: a change or addition to the Constitution.
Official sources:
- USAGov: Branches of the U.S. government
- National Archives: The Constitution of the United States (transcript)
- National Archives: The Bill of Rights (transcript)
Try it now: Practice: name the branch or right. 1) The Senate votes on the president's choice for a federal judge. 2) The Supreme Court rules that a law breaks the Constitution. 3) A newspaper prints a story criticizing the mayor. 4) The president signs a bill into law. Answers: 1) Legislative checking the executive. 2) Judicial checking the legislative. 3) Freedom of the press, First Amendment. 4) Executive (carrying out its role in making a law).
You can now name the three branches, explain checks and balances in a scenario, and connect a situation to the Bill of Rights.

check.why: Congress, the legislative branch, makes laws.

check.q: The Supreme Court rules a law unconstitutional. What is this an example of?
options: A check by the judicial branch on the legislative branch
check.why: Courts can overturn laws that conflict with the Constitution.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Cause, effect and evidence in history
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Identify a cause and an effect in a historical event and the evidence that supports an inference.
This lesson builds toward: Given a historical event or argument, you will identify a cause and an effect and the evidence that supports an inference, with the evidence named from the source.
History questions often ask why something happened (the cause) and what happened because of it (the effect). Signal words: because, so, as a result, led to, therefore, due to.
Worked example. "In the late 1800s, factories in cities offered many new jobs. As a result, millions of people moved from farms to cities. City populations grew fast, and crowded housing became a problem." Cause: factory jobs in cities. Effect: people moved to cities. A later effect: crowded housing. One cause can lead to a chain of effects.
An inference is a conclusion the evidence supports. GED questions may ask which statement from a source supports an inference. Pick the statement that gives proof, not just one that is about the same topic.
Be careful: two things happening at the same time does not always mean one caused the other. Look for the source to say or show the link.
Step by step:
- Find the event the question asks about.
- Look for signal words: because, so, as a result, led to.
- Name the cause (why) and the effect (what happened next).
- For an inference, pick the statement that gives proof for it.
- Check the source actually links the two; do not assume.
Words to know:
- Cause: why something happened.
- Effect: what happened because of the cause.
- Inference: a conclusion supported by evidence.
- Industrialization: the growth of factories and machines making goods.
Try it now: Practice: "The 1930s Dust Bowl destroyed crops on the Great Plains. Many farm families lost their land and moved west to look for work." 1) Cause? 2) Effect? 3) Which statement best supports the inference "the Dust Bowl changed where people lived": (a) "The Dust Bowl destroyed crops" or (b) "Many farm families moved west"? Answers: 1) Dust storms destroyed crops. 2) Families lost land and moved west. 3) (b): it shows people moving.
You can now find causes and effects in history and choose the evidence that supports an inference.

check.q: "Gas prices rose sharply, so more people took the bus." What is the effect?
check.why: Taking the bus is what happened because gas prices rose.

check.q: Which statement best supports the inference that a new highway helped a town's businesses?
options: "Store sales in town doubled in the five years after the highway opened."
check.why: It gives evidence of business growth linked to the highway.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Economics and graphs
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Read a chart or map, describe the trend and choose the conclusion the data supports.
This lesson builds toward: Given a map, chart or graph about history, economics or geography, you will read values, describe a trend and choose the conclusion the data supports, without adding facts that are not shown.
Supply is how much of something is for sale. Demand is how much people want to buy. When demand goes up and supply stays the same, prices usually rise. When supply goes up and demand stays the same, prices usually fall. Example: after a freeze ruins orange crops, the supply of oranges drops and prices rise.
Graphs: read the title, the labels and the units first. Practice table (made up): a city's unemployment rate was 8% in 2020, 6% in 2021, 5% in 2022 and 4% in 2023. Trend: falling each year. Supported conclusion: a smaller share of people looking for work had no job in 2023 than in 2020. Not supported: why it fell, because the table does not say.
Maps: read the title, the legend (key) and the compass rose. The legend tells you what colors or symbols mean. A map of rainfall might use darker colors for more rain. Use the scale to estimate distance.
Percent change is common: from 8% to 4% is a drop of 4 percentage points. You can use the on-screen calculator for the math.
Step by step:
- Read the title, labels, units or the map legend.
- Find the value the question asks about.
- Describe the trend: rising, falling or no clear pattern.
- Pick the conclusion that stays inside the data.
- For prices, ask: did supply or demand change?
Words to know:
- Supply: how much of a good or service is for sale.
- Demand: how much of it people want to buy.
- Unemployment rate: the share of people looking for work who do not have a job.
- Legend: the key on a map or chart that tells what colors or symbols mean.
- Percentage point: the simple difference between two percents, like 8% to 4% is 4 points.
Try it now: Practice (made-up data): a bar chart shows average monthly rent in a city: 2019: $1,000; 2021: $1,150; 2023: $1,400. 1) Rent in 2021? 2) Trend? 3) How much did rent rise from 2019 to 2023? 4) Which conclusion is supported: (a) rent rose over this time, or (b) rent rose because of new jobs? Answers: 1) $1,150. 2) Rising. 3) $400. 4) (a); the chart does not show why.
You can now use supply and demand to explain price changes, and read charts and maps to pick a supported conclusion.

check.q: A storm destroys many lumber mills, so less lumber is for sale while builders still want it. What usually happens to lumber prices?
check.why: Supply fell while demand stayed the same, so prices usually rise.

check.q: On a map, what tells you what each color means?
check.why: The legend explains colors and symbols.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Putting it together: analyzing a founding document
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Complete a source analysis sheet on a founding document.
This lesson builds toward: Given a primary or secondary source, you will identify the main idea, the author's point of view, and which statements are facts and which are opinions, pointing to the words that show each answer. Given a short civics scenario, you will explain which branch of government acts and how checks and balances or a constitutional right apply, getting at least 4 of 5 right. Given a historical event or argument, you will identify a cause and an effect and the evidence that supports an inference, with the evidence named from the source.
GED questions often give you a short piece of an old document and ask about its main idea, its purpose or how it connects to government today. The Preamble, the opening sentence of the Constitution, is a good one to practice with. Read it on the National Archives website.
The Preamble begins "We the People of the United States" and lists goals: to form a more perfect union, establish justice, insure domestic tranquility (peace at home), provide for the common defense, promote the general welfare (the well-being of all) and secure the blessings of liberty.
Worked analysis. Who and when: delegates to the Constitutional Convention, 1787. Type: primary source. Main idea: the people set up a government to meet shared goals. Point of view: leaders who wanted a stronger national government than they had before. Cause and effect: the earlier government under the Articles of Confederation was weak, which led to writing a new Constitution. Branches: the Preamble introduces the whole Constitution, which sets up all three branches.
Your sheet does not need perfect answers. It needs answers you can support by pointing to the words in the document.
Step by step:
- Open the Constitution transcript on archives.gov and read the Preamble.
- Write who wrote it, when, and whether it is primary or secondary.
- Write the main idea in one sentence and the point of view.
- Write one fact about it and one goal or opinion in it.
- Write one cause and one effect, and the branch or right it connects to.
- Add your dated study plan at the bottom.
Words to know:
- Preamble: the opening sentence of the Constitution that states its purpose.
- Articles of Confederation: the first plan of US government, used before the Constitution.
- Domestic tranquility: peace at home.
- General welfare: the well-being of all the people.
Official sources:
- National Archives: The Constitution of the United States (transcript)
- National Archives: The Bill of Rights (transcript)
Try it now: Final task: complete your one-page source analysis sheet on the Preamble (or the Bill of Rights) from archives.gov, using the steps above. Add your dated GED study plan at the bottom, then score your work with the course rubric.
You can now analyze a founding document: its source type, main idea, point of view, causes and effects, and links to how government works.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Source and point of view Source type or author is wrong or missing. Correct author, date and source type, and a point of view that fits who wrote it and why. Also explains how the point of view shapes what the document says. Main idea, fact and opinion The main idea is wrong, or fact and opinion are mixed up. A correct one-sentence main idea, one fact and one goal or opinion, each tied to the words. Quotes the exact words that show each answer. Cause and effect No cause or effect, or they are reversed. One correct cause and one correct effect connected to the document. Shows a chain: a cause, an effect and a later effect. Government connection No branch or right named, or the wrong one. Names the branch or right it relates to and explains why in one sentence. Also gives an example of checks and balances or a right in use today. Data reading Did not complete the graph practice in Lesson 5. Completed the Lesson 5 graph practice with a conclusion that stays inside the data. Also explains a price change using supply and demand. Study plan No study plan, or no dates. A study plan with at least one date each week through the target test week. Also includes a date for GED Ready or a booked test date. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, reread that part of the document and fix your answer.

check.q: The Preamble was written in 1787 by delegates to the Constitutional Convention. What kind of source is it?
check.why: It was made at the time by the people who wrote the Constitution.

check.q: The Articles of Confederation created a weak national government. What was one effect?
options: The Bill of Rights was removed
check.why: The weakness of the Articles led to the Constitution of 1787.
